title: CBP Flew a Drone Over Minneapolis Protests in 2020, Linked Sources Report
description_short: CBP Flew a Drone Over Minneapolis Protests in 2020, Linked Sources Report
description_medium: A People’s History Museum guest post reports that U.S. Customs and Border Protection flew a military-grade drone over Minneapolis during 2020 protests after George Floyd’s murder. It says CBP also piloted surveillance aircraft over demonstrations in Washington, D.C., and 13 other cities, and that federal agents could view live footage and store it for possible criminal investigations.
description_long: A People’s History Museum guest post published April 1, 2021 reports that, during 2020 protests against police brutality and systemic racism after George Floyd’s murder, U.S. Customs and Border Protection flew a military-grade drone over Minneapolis and piloted surveillance aircraft over demonstrations in Washington, D.C., and 13 other cities. The post says federal agents could view live aerial footage on their phones and store it for potential use in criminal investigations. The linked Erasmus University and Privacy International pieces discuss broader protest surveillance, including facial recognition and digital evidence, and examples outside the United States. The PHM post supplies the U.S.-specific agency, protest context and technology absent from the earlier account. It is a guest blog, which the page says is not curated and need not reflect the museum’s views. It attributes the activity to CBP but does not report a presidential order or Trump’s personal role. The description is limited to the reported agency activity during 2020.
notes: Focused reads: Privacy International’s January 10, 2025 article describes surveillance in Colombia, France and India; Erasmus University’s article discusses protest technology, privacy and chilling effects; People’s History Museum’s April 1, 2021 guest post specifically reports CBP’s military-grade drone over Minneapolis during 2020 protests and surveillance aircraft over Washington, D.C., and 13 other cities, with federal agents able to view/store footage. The PHM page labels guest posts uncurated and says they may not reflect the museum’s view. This supports a U.S. agency deployment during 2020, but not a direction or order by President Trump. The title and descriptions are narrowed to the reported conduct.
proposed_correction: Provide a U.S.-specific source documenting the agency, surveillance tools, affected protests and deployment date, then revise the existing long description to remove unsubstantiated claims.

title: Council for National Policy List Compiles More Than 1,000 Names
description_short: Council for National Policy List Compiles More Than 1,000 Names
description_medium: The Council for National Policy formed in 1981 as a private forum for conservative organizers, donors and activists. A later Trump Timeline page compiled 1,011 names from 1981 to 2020 and acknowledged that the list might include fewer than half of the council’s members. The compilation does not establish that Donald Trump belonged to the group.
description_long: The Council for National Policy began in 1981 as a private forum for conservative organizers, donors and activists. A contemporaneous New York Times report described more than 50 conservatives gathering to form an umbrella organization they hoped would gain influence. Decades later, a Trump Timeline page published a list of 1,011 names spanning 1981 through 2020 and acknowledged that it might include fewer than half of the council’s members. Because the compilation is incomplete and covers many years, it does not show when a person joined or what role that person played. The synopsis names figures such as Charlie Kirk and Kellyanne Conway, but does not establish Donald Trump’s membership or participation. Nor does the list tie the council’s activity to a specific Trump policy or campaign action. A partial name list alone cannot establish influence over a policy or coordination with a president.

title: Donald Trump sues the U.S. government for discrimination
description_short: Donald Trump sues the U.S. government for discrimination
description_medium: In 1993, Donald Trump sued the federal government over the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, arguing that the law favored tribal casinos and disadvantaged casino owners such as himself. The supplied account says he also challenged the law on states’ rights grounds and sought to block tribal casinos. It does not provide the court’s decision or the case’s later procedural history.
description_long: Donald Trump filed a federal lawsuit in 1993 challenging the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, the 1988 law governing tribal gaming. As summarized in the supplied account, Trump argued that the law discriminated against him as a casino owner by allowing Native American tribes to open casinos, and he also claimed it infringed states’ rights. The New York Times headline linked to the record says the suit sought to block Indian casinos. These are arguments attributed to Trump’s complaint, not a judicial finding that the statute discriminated against him or violated states’ rights. The record does not identify the specific tribal parties, lay out the complete legal arguments, or show how the court resolved the dispute. Its linked Times report returned HTTP 403 in a focused read, and the supplied draft contained no ruling or docket details. The filing can be described as a challenge to tribal gaming under federal law, but the outcome and the court’s reasoning remain unknown from the available material. A fuller account needs the complaint or docket and a reliable source on the procedural disposition before it can say whether the suit was dismissed, decided on the merits or otherwise concluded.
